But this general rule, the fact that state of origin (or citizenship) did not matter when selecting players from other nations, was NOT applied for the UK. For the 1904 match against Ireland, English and Welsh players in selection were considered, as for the previous fixtures in 1899, 1901 and 1902, not to have satisfied the requirements of representation for Scotland and were not selected for the trial, which the WRU was unhappy with.[7] Despite this, Welsh-born and capped, Ted Gwynne, was not selected for either the Welsh trials nor the final match. However, Scottish-born and future-capped, Ernest F. Ffennell (Oxford University) played in the 'Probables' team. English-born R.B. Louson (Lansdowne), also capped by Ireland in 1893, played for the 'Possibles'.[8] For the next five international clashes against Ireland (1907-1912 inclusive), only Scottish-born players were selected.

The last matches between the two nations were played on 15 March 1913, but there is no evidence this restriction on non-Scottish born players was a continuing official union policy up to 1913, only for the six selected years (1899, 1901-02, 1907-09 & 1912).[9] This selection policy, only allowing Scottish-born players, directly cost the team the potential representation of key "Scots" such as Charles Burton (capper for Blackheath), J. E. Crabbie, John Biggar, J. T. Thompson, Arthur Brown, Frederick Henderson and Ronald MacLachlan, some whom had played previously for the national team. While it could be argued this rule cost Scotland victories, the impact is hard to measure accurately. Of the six matches played under these rules, Scotland won two and lost four. All games were narrow, except for the 1909 encounter, where they lost by 12 points, their worst performance during that specific period.
